# Tidal Locking and Its Profound Influence on Planetary Climates

Tidal locking occurs when a planet's rotation period matches its orbital period, causing one hemisphere to face its star permanently. This phenomenon, common among planets orbiting red dwarf stars, creates some of the most extreme and fascinating climates in the universe.

The most obvious consequence is the dramatic temperature contrast between hemispheres. The dayside, bathed in perpetual starlight, can reach temperatures hot enough to vaporize rock on close-orbiting worlds, while the nightside plunges to frigid extremes where atmospheres may freeze out entirely. On the exoplanet WASP-121b, dayside temperatures exceed 2,500°C, while some models suggest nightside temperatures hundreds of degrees cooler.

However, tidal locking doesn't necessarily doom a planet to climatic extremes. Atmospheric circulation can redistribute heat remarkably effectively. On temperate tidally locked worlds, powerful winds transport energy from the dayside to the nightside, moderating temperatures on both sides. Climate models suggest that with sufficient atmospheric pressure—perhaps one bar or more—a tidally locked planet could maintain liquid water on its dayside while preventing atmospheric collapse on its nightside.

This heat transport creates unique weather patterns. Simulations predict a permanent day-night terminator zone where opposing air masses collide, potentially generating perpetual storms and precipitation. The dayside likely features a massive, persistent hurricane-like structure at the substellar point, where intense heating drives powerful updrafts
